targets.label: Lemma 6
targets.statement:
Lemma 6 For an MDP with rewards $r^{k}(s,a)$ and transition probability $\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)$ such that $\|\tilde{P}(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\|_{1}\leq\epsilon_{s,a},$ the Bellman error $B_{\pi_{e}}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)$ for state-action pair s, a is upper bounded as

$$
\begin{array}{r}{B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)\leq\left\|\tilde{P}(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\right\|_{1}\|h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(\cdot)\|_{\infty},\quad|B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)|\leq\tilde{D}\operatorname*{min}\left\{\epsilon_{s,a},2\right\},}\end{array}\tag{28}
$$

where $\tilde{D}\geq 0$ is an upper bound on the diameter of the MDP with transition probability $\tilde{P}$ and on the span of the bias, $h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s)-h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})\leq\tilde{D}$ for all $s,s^{\prime}$

targets.label: Lemma 11
targets.statement:
Lemma 11 (Bounded Span of MDP) For an MDP $\mathcal{M}$ with rewards $r^{k}(s,a)$ and transition probabilities P, for any stationary policy π with average reward $\lambda_{\pi}^{k}$ , the difference of bias of any two states $s,$ and $s^{\prime},$ is upper bounded by the diameter of the MDP D as:

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)-h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})\leq D~\forall~s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}.\tag{102}
$$

targets.label: Lemma 7
targets.statement: Lemma 7 For any $1 \leq t \leq T$ , the probability that the event $\mathcal{E}_{t}$ fails to occur us upper bounded by $\frac{1}{20t^{6}}$

nl_proof:
### Proof of Lemma 6

Proof Starting with the definition of Bellman error in Equation (26), we get

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)=\underset{\gamma\to 1}{\operatorname*{lim}}(Q_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)-(r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})))}\\ &{\quad\quad\quad\quad=\underset{\gamma\to 1}{\operatorname*{lim}}((r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime}))-(r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})))}\end{array}\tag{128}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}(\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)-P(s^{\prime}|s,a))V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})\tag{129}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}\gamma(\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}(\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)-P(s^{\prime}|s,a))V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})+V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s)-V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s))\tag{130}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}\gamma\Bigg(\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}(\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)-P(s^{\prime}|s,a))V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})-\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s)
$$

$$
+\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s)\bigg)\tag{131}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}\gamma(\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}(\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)-P(s^{\prime}|s,a))(V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})-V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s)))\tag{132}
$$

$$
=\left(\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\left(\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)-P(s^{\prime}|s,a)\right)\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}\gamma\left(V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})-V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s)\right)\right)\tag{133}
$$

$$
=\left(\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}\left(\tilde{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)-P(s^{\prime}|s,a)\right)h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s^{\prime})\right)\tag{134}
$$

$$
\leq\left\|\tilde{P}(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\right\|_{1}\|h_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(\cdot)\|_{\infty}\tag{135}
$$

$$
\le\epsilon_{s,a}\tilde{D}\tag{136}
$$

where Equation (129) comes from the assumption that the rewards are known to the agent. Equation (133) follows from the fact that the difference between value function at two states is bounded. Equation (134) comes from the definition of bias term Puterman (1994) where h is the bias of the policy π when run on the sampled MDP. Equation (135) follows from Hölder's inequality. In Equation (136), $\|h(\cdot)\|_{\infty}$ is bounded by the diameter $\tilde{D}$ of the sampled MDP(from Lemma 11). Also, the $\ell_{1}$ norm of probability vector difference is bounded from the definition.

Additionally, note that the $\ell_{1}$ norm in Equation (135) is bounded by 2. Thus the Bellman error is loose upper bounded by $2 \tilde{D}$ for all state-action pairs.

### Proof of Lemma 11

Proof Consider two states $s,s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}$ . Also, let $\tau$ be a random variable defined as:

$$
\tau=\operatorname*{min}\{t\geq 1:S_{t}=s^{\prime},S_{1}=s\}\tag{103}
$$

Then, for any policy π, we have the following Bellman operator

$$
\begin{array}{c}{{h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)=r_{\pi}^{k}(s)-\lambda_{\pi}^{k}+ <P_{\pi}(\cdot|s),h_{\pi}^{P,k}>}}\\ {{=Th_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)(s)}}\end{array}\tag{104}
$$

where $\begin{array}{r}{P_{\pi}(s^{\prime}|s)=\sum_{a}\pi(a|s)P(s^{\prime}|s,a)}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{r}{r_{\pi}^{k}(s)=\sum_{a}\pi(a|s)r^{k}(s,a)}\end{array}$

We also define another operator,

$$
\bar{T}h(s)=\left\{\begin{array}{l l}{\operatorname*{min}_{s,a}r^{k}(s,a)-\lambda_{\pi}^{k}+ <P_{\pi}(\cdot|s),h>,}&{s\neq s^{\prime}}\\ {h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime}),}&{s=s^{\prime}}\end{array}\right.\tag{105}
$$

Note that $\begin{array}{r}{(T-\bar{T})h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)=r_{\pi}^{k}(s,a)-\operatorname*{min}_{s,a}r^{k}(s,a)\geq 0}\end{array}$ ,for all s. Hence, we have $\bar{T}h(s)\leq Th(s)=h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)$ , for all s. Further, for any two vectors $u,v,$ where all the elements of u are not smaller than w we have $\bar{T}u \geq \bar{T}w$ . Hence, we have ${\bar{T}}^{n}h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)\leq h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)$ for all s. Unrolling the recurrence, we have

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)\geq\bar{T}^{n}h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)=\mathbb{E}\left[-(\lambda_{\pi}^{k}-\operatorname*{min}_{s,a}r^{k}(s,a))(n\wedge\tau)+h_{\pi}^{P,k}(S_{n\wedge\tau})\right]\tag{106}
$$

For lim $n \to \infty$ , we have $h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)\geq h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})-D$ , completing the proof.

### Proof of Lemma 7

Proof From the result of Weissman et al. (2003), the $\ell_{1}$ distance of a probability distribution over S events with n samples is bounded as:

$$
\begin{array}{r l r}&{}&{\mathbb{P}\left(\|P(\cdot|s,a)-\hat{P}(\cdot|s,a)\|_{1}\geq\epsilon\right)\leq(2^{S}-2)\exp\left(-\displaystyle\frac{n(s,a)\epsilon^{2}}{2}\right)}\\ &{}&{\leq(2^{S})\exp\left(-\displaystyle\frac{n(s,a)\epsilon^{2}}{2}\right)~}\end{array}\tag{137}
$$

Thus, for $\begin{array}{r}{\epsilon=\sqrt{\frac{2}{n(s,a)}\log(2^{S}20SAt^{7})}\le\sqrt{\frac{14S}{n(s,a)}\log(2At)}\le\sqrt{\frac{14S}{n(s,a)}\log(2AT)}}\end{array}$ , we have

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\|P(\cdot|s,a)-\hat{P}(\cdot|s,a)\|_{1}\geq\sqrt{\frac{14S}{n(s,a)}\log(2At)}\right)\leq(2^{S})\exp\left(-\frac{n(s,a)}{2}\frac{2}{n(s,a)}\log(2^{S}20SAt^{7})\right)\tag{138}
$$

$$
=2^{S}\frac{1}{2^{S}20SAt^{7}}\tag{139}
$$

$$
={\frac{1}{20ASt^{7}}}\tag{140}
$$

We sum over the all the possible values of $n(s,a)$ till t time-step to bound the probability that the event $\mathcal{E}_{t}$ does not occur as:

$$
\sum_{n(s,a)=1}^{t}{\frac{1}{20SAt^{7}}}\leq{\frac{1}{20SAt^{6}}}\tag{141}
$$

Finally, summing over all the $s,a,$ we get

$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\|P(\cdot|s,a)-\hat{P}(\cdot|s,a)\|_{1}\geq\sqrt{\frac{14S}{n(s,a)}\log(2At)}\ \forall s,a\right)\leq\frac{1}{20t^{6}}\tag{142}
$$

context.name: Setup: MDP, rewards, policy and average reward (Section 3)
context.statement:
We consider an infinite horizon discounted Markov decision process (MDP) $\mathcal{M}$ defined by the tuple $\left(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r^{1},r^{2},\cdot\cdot\cdot,r^{K},\rho_{0}\right)$ . $\mathcal{S}$ denotes a finite set of state space of size S, and $\mathcal{A}$ denotes a finite set of A actions. $P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]^{S}$ denotes the probability transition distribution. K denotes the number of objectives and $[K]=\{1,2,\cdots,K\}$ is the set of K objectives. Let $r^{k}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ be the bounded reward function for objective $k \in [ K ]$. Lastly, $\rho_{0}:\mathcal{S}\to [0,1]$ is the distribution of initial state. We motivate our choice of bounds on rewards from the fact that many problems in practice require explicit reward shaping. Hence, the controller or the learner is aware of the bounds on the rewards. We consider the bounds to be [0, 1] for our case which is easy to satisfy by reward shaping.

We use a stochastic policy $\pi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to [0,1]$ which returns the probability of selecting action $a \in{\mathcal{A}}$ for any given state $s \in{\mathcal{S}}$. Following policy π on the MDP, the agent observes a sequence of random variables $\{S_{t}, A_{t}\}_{t}$ where $S_{t}$ denotes the state of the agent at time t and $A_{t}$ denotes the action taken by the agent at time t. The expected discounted long term reward and expected per step reward of the objective k are given by $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ , respectively, when the joint policy π is followed. Formally, for discount factor $\gamma\in(0,1)$ , $J_{\pi}^{P,k}$ and $\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}$ are defined as

$$
J_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{1}
$$

$$
S_{0}\sim\rho_{0}(S_{0}),\ A_{t}\sim\pi(A_{t}|S_{t}),\ S_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})
$$

$$
\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{S_{0},A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\frac{1}{\tau}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})]\tag{2}
$$

$$
=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}(1-\gamma)J_{\pi}^{P,k}\tag{3}
$$

context.name: Bias Bellman equation, eq. (4)
context.statement:
Equation (3) follows from the Laurent series expansion of $J_{\pi}^{k}$ (Puterman, 1994). For brevity, in the rest of the paper $\mathbb{E}_{S_{t}, A_{t}, S_{t + 1}; t \geq 0}[ \cdot ]$ will be denoted as $\mathbb{E}_{\rho,\pi,P}[\cdot]$ , where $S_{0}\sim \rho_{0}, \ A_{t}\sim$ $\pi(\cdot|S_{t}),\ S_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})$ . The expected per step reward satisfies the following Bellman equation

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)+\lambda_{\pi}^{P,k}=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}\left[r^{k}(s,a)\right]+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}\left[\sum_{s^{\prime}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})\right]\tag{4}
$$

where $h_{\pi}^{k}(s)$ is the bias of policy π for state s.

context.name: Discounted value and Q-functions, eqs. (5)-(6)
context.statement:
We also define the discounted value function $V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s)$ and Q-value functions $Q_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s,a)$ as follows:

$$
V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{A_{0},S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})|S_{0}=s]\tag{5}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l}{{Q_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{S_{1},A_{1},\cdots}[\displaystyle\operatorname*{lim}_{\tau\to\infty}\sum_{t=0}^{\tau}\gamma^{t}r^{k}(S_{t},A_{t})\vert S_{0}=s,A_{0}=a]}}\\ {{\mathrm{~}=r^{k}(s,a)+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}[\displaystyle\sum_{s^{\prime}}P(s^{\prime}\vert s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s^{\prime})]}}\end{array}\tag{6}
$$

context.name: Bias vs. discounted value, eq. (7)
context.statement:
Further, the bias $h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s)$ and the value function $V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}$ are related as

$$
h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s_{1})-h_{\pi}^{P,k}(s_{2})=\operatorname*{lim}_{\gamma\to 1}(V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s_{1})-V_{\gamma,\pi}^{P,k}(s_{2})),{\mathrm{~w h e r e~}}s_{1},s_{2}\in{\mathcal{S}}.\tag{7}
$$

For notation simplicity, we may drop the superscript P when discussing about variables for the true MDP.

context.name: Induced Markov chain and Definition 1 (Diameter), eq. (8)
context.statement:
Note that each policy induces a Markov Chain on the states $\mathcal{S}$ with transition probabilities $\begin{array}{r}{P_{\pi,s}(s^{\prime})=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\pi(a|s)P(s^{\prime}|s,a)}\end{array}$ . After defining a policy, we can now define the diameter of the MDP $\mathcal{M}$ as:

Definition 1 (Diameter) Consider the Markov Chain induced by the policy π on the MDP $\mathcal{M}$. Let $T(s^{\prime}|\mathcal{M},\pi,s)$ be a random variable that denotes the first time step when this Markov Chain enters state s' starting from state s. Then, the diameter of the MDP $\mathcal{M}$ is defined as:

$$
D(\mathcal{M})=\operatorname*{max}_{\pi}\operatorname*{max}_{s^{\prime}\neq s}\mathbb{E}\left[T(s^{\prime}|\mathcal{M},\pi,s)\right]\tag{8}
$$

context.name: Assumption 1 (ergodic MDP), eq. (9)
context.statement:
Further, starting from an arbitrary initial state distribution, the state distribution may take a while to converge to the steady state distribution. For any policy π, let $P_{\pi,s}^{t}=(P_{\pi,s})^{t}$ be the t-step probability distribution of the states when policy π is applied to MDP with transition probabilities P starting from state s.

We are now ready to state our first assumption on the MDP. We assume that the Markov Decision Process is ergodic. This implies that: 1. for any policy all states, $s \in{\mathcal{S}}$ communicate with each other; 2. for any policy, the process converges to the steady state distribution exponentially fast. Formally, we have

Assumption 1 The Markov Decision Process, $\mathcal{M}$, is ergodic. Then, we have,

1. The diameter, D, of $\mathcal{M}$ is finite.

2. For any policy π, for some $C > 0$ and $0 \leq \rho < 1$ , we have

$$
\|P_{\pi,s}^{t}-d_{\pi}\|_{TV}\leq C\rho^{t}\tag{9}
$$

where $d_{\pi}$ is the steady state distribution induced by policy π on the MDP.

context.name: Bellman error, eq. (26)
context.statement:
To compute the regret incurred by the optimal policy $\pi_{e}$ for the sampled MDP on the true MDP ${\mathcal{M}},$ we use Bellman error. For some policy $\pi,$ we define Bellman error $B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)$ for the infinite horizon MDPs as the difference between the cumulative expected rewards obtained for deviating from the system model with transition $\tilde{P}$ for one step by taking action a in state s and then following policy π. We have:

$$
\begin{array}{r l}&{B_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)=\left(Q_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)-r(s,a)-\gamma\sum_{s^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}P(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)\right)}\\ &{B_{\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)=\underset{\gamma\to 1}{\operatorname*{lim}}B_{\gamma,\pi}^{\tilde{P},k}(s,a)}\end{array}\tag{26}
$$

context.name: Good event E_t, eq. (29), and empirical estimates
context.statement:
A major part of the regret analysis is how well the learned model estimates the true system model. For that, bound the deviation of the estimates of the estimated transition probabilities of the Markov Decision Processes $\mathcal{M}$. For that we use $\ell_{1}$ deviation bounds from (Weissman et al., 2003). Consider, the following event,

$$
\mathcal{E}_{t}=\left\{\|\bar{P}_{t}(\cdot|s,a)-P(\cdot|s,a)\|_{1}\leq\sqrt{\frac{14S\log(2AT)}{\operatorname*{max}\{1,n_{t}(s,a)\}}}\forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\right\}\tag{29}
$$

where $\begin{array}{r}{n_{t}(s,a)=\sum_{t^{\prime}=1}^{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{S_{t^{\prime}}=s,a_{t^{\prime}}=a\}}}\end{array}$ and $\begin{array}{r}{\bar{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a)=\left(\sum_{t^{\prime}=1}^{t}\mathbf{1}_{\{S_{t^{\prime}}=s,a_{t^{\prime}}=a,S_{t^{\prime}+1}=s^{\prime}\}}\right)/n_{t}(s,a)}\end{array}$ of the empirical estimate of the transition probabilities.

context.name: Algorithm 1 (Model-Based Joint Decision Making) and its description (Section 5.1)
context.statement:
Algorithm 1 Model-Based Joint Decision Making Algorithm   
1: procedure Model Based Online($\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},[K],f,r$)   
2: Initialize $N(s,a,s^{\prime})=1\forall(s,a,s^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}$   
3: Initialize $\nu_{0}(s,a)=0~\forall~(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$   
4: Initialize $\textstyle\pi_{1}(a|s)={\frac{1}{|{\mathcal{A}}|}}\forall(a,s)\in{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{S}}$   
5: Initialize $e = 1$   
6: for time steps $t=1,2,\cdots$ do   
7: Observe current state $S_{t}$   
8: Sample action to play $A_{t}\sim\pi_{e}(\cdot|S_{t})$   
9: Play $A_{t},$ obtain reward $r_{t}\in [0,1]^{K}$ and observe next state $S_{t + 1}$   
10: Update $N(S_{t},A_{t},S_{t+1})\gets N(S_{t},A_{t},S_{t+1})+1,\nu_{e}(S_{t},A_{t})\gets\nu_{e}(S_{t},A_{t})+1$   
11: if $\begin{array}{r}{\nu_{e}(S_{t},A_{t})\ge\operatorname*{max}\{1,\sum_{e^{\prime}<e}\nu_{e^{\prime}}(S_{t},A_{t})\}}\end{array}$ then   
12: Update epoch counter $e \gets e + 1$   
13: Initialize $\nu_{e}(s,a)=0~\forall~(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}$   
14: $P_{e}(s^{\prime}|s,a)\sim Dir(N(s,a,\cdot))\ \forall\ (s,a)$   
15: Solve steady state distribution $d(s,a)$ as the solution of the optimization   
problem in Equations (20-23)   
16: Obtain optimal policy $\pi_{e}$ as   
$\pi_{e}(a|s)={\frac{d(s,a)}{\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}d(s,a)}}$   
17: end if   
18: end for   
19: end procedure

Algorithm 1 describes the overall procedure that estimates the transition probabilities and the reward functions. The algorithm takes as input the state space $\mathcal{S}$, action space ${\mathcal{A}},$ set of agents [K], the reward structure $r$, and the objective function $f .$ It initializes the next state visit count for each state-action pair $N(s,a,s^{\prime})$ by one for Dirichlet sampling. For initial exploration, the policy uses a uniform distribution over all the actions. The algorithm proceeds in epochs e with $t_{e}$ denoting the time step t at which epoch e starts. Also, $\nu_{e}(s,a)$ stores the number of times a state-action pair is visited in epoch e. We assume that the controller is optimizing for infinite horizon and thus there is no stopping condition for epoch loop in Line 6. For each time index $t \in [ t_{e}, t_{e + 1})$ in epoch $e,$ the controller observes the state, samples and plays the action according to $\pi_{e}(\cdot|s)$ , and observes the rewards for each agent and next state. It then updates the state visit count for the observed state and played action pair. We break the current epoch e if the total number of visitations of any state action pair in current epoch exceeds total visitations in previous epoch. This epoch breaking strategy ensures that each state-action triggers epoch switches exponentially slower. This increasing epoch duration bounds the policy switching cost (Jaksch et al., 2010). After breaking the epoch, we sample transition probabilities from the updated posterior and find a new optimal policy for the sampled MDP by solving the optimization framework described in Equation(20).
